name: The capstone round, scored
note: Moments from a mock AI-assisted round. Each tests whether the whole loop survives time pressure and an interviewer watching. Pick the rubric-maximizing move.

items.prompt: Capstone round, minute 1. The strongest opening move is:
candidates: Restate the problem, confirm the one ambiguity, and say the invariants you'll commit before prompting — clarify + preregister + communication in the first minute, the three the rubric weights most under pressure
Start prompting immediately to show speed
Write the whole solution by hand to prove you don't need AI
Ask which model you're allowed to use
items.correct: Restate the problem, confirm the one ambiguity, and say the invariants you'll commit before prompting — clarify + preregister + communication in the first minute, the three the rubric weights most under pressure
items.explanation: The first minute is where clarify, preregister, and narration pay off most — and exactly where pressure makes people skip them. Opening with them sets the tone for the whole round and front-loads the highest-scoring behaviours.
items.principle: Spend minute one on clarify, preregister, and saying so — the stages pressure makes you skip.

items.prompt: The interviewer asks 'why this approach?' about AI-generated code. The rubric-maximizing answer:
candidates: Explain the design in your own words and what you verified it against — demonstrating comprehension (you read it) and rigor (you checked it), which is exactly what the question probes
'That's how the AI implemented it.' — cedes comprehension and ownership
'It passes the tests.' — rigor with no comprehension
Re-read the code silently for a while, then guess
items.correct: Explain the design in your own words and what you verified it against — demonstrating comprehension (you read it) and rigor (you checked it), which is exactly what the question probes
items.explanation: The follow-up is a comprehension-and-ownership test. Answering from your own understanding — not from the AI's authorship — is the signal; 'the AI did it' and 'the tests pass' each concede half of what's being scored.
items.principle: Answer 'why this approach' from your understanding, not the AI's authorship.

items.prompt: The capstone problem is one you've never seen. What actually transfers?
candidates: The loop — clarify, preregister, prompt, read, verify, explain — is problem-independent, and the rubric dimensions are what's scored on any AI-assisted task, so the process carries even when the problem is novel
Nothing — each problem needs its own memorized approach
Only if you happen to have seen a similar problem before
The specific prompt that worked on the last problem
items.correct: The loop — clarify, preregister, prompt, read, verify, explain — is problem-independent, and the rubric dimensions are what's scored on any AI-assisted task, so the process carries even when the problem is novel
items.explanation: The whole bet of the guide is transfer: the loop and the rubric are problem-independent, so they carry to unseen problems — which is exactly what interviews (and real work) throw at you.
items.principle: The loop transfers; memorized solutions don't — that's the point of learning the process.
